stories.topic: Vajpayee's Speech On The Knowledge Economy
stories.summary: Ajay recalls a Vajpayee speech (around 2002 or 2003) with beautiful paragraphs arguing that the knowledge economy is not something to hide in a university. Knowledge should fill every pore of our bodies, cast aside individual superstition, feed into firms to make them high-productivity, and feed into the state so it does evidence-based policy instead of crude electoral brutality.
stories.insight: An aspirational frame for what the state should be. Even when politics looks like nothing more than seizing coercive power to help friends and harm rivals, we should appeal to the better angels of ourselves rather than settle. Knowledge diffusing into firms, the state and individual lives is the elevated alternative to underdevelopment.

stories.summary: Ajay invokes the model of Albert Einstein who, while a full-time clerk in a patent office with no funding and no budgets, did some of the most influential science ever. The mind-numbing day job did not extinguish his inner fire of curiosity and passion for knowledge for its own sake.
stories.insight: The romantic model of the scholar is internally driven curiosity, not journal-paper-as-career-rung. When the system selects for Einsteins it gets Einsteins; when it selects for grade-grabbers gaming citation systems, that is what it gets. The institutions can recover only if they remember whom they exist to serve.

stories.summary: Ajay's friend Josh Felman told him that putting one child through college in America involves buying one brand-new BMW car every year and rolling it off the edge of a cliff. Universities have figured out that parents crave the brand name and have started charging accordingly, then plowing the money into resorts, gyms, luxurious housing and five-star facilities rather than knowledge.
stories.insight: The implicit bargain is no longer education, it is daycare-plus-credential. Parents get four years of supervised storage and a chhaap; kids get a job at the end. The kindling of imagination, the intellectual journey, has been pushed aside because no one in the transaction is paying for it.

stories.topic: The Indian PhD Selection Wastes Seed Corn
stories.summary: Ajay argues the deepest damage in academia is done at the gate. Indian PhD admissions demand objective exams and high college grades, so the people selected are the most predictable, safe, respectable, regimented bureaucrats. The curiosity-and-passion types who would have been the next Einstein or Ramanujan are screened out before they begin.
stories.insight: The selectors are the root cause. Whatever incentives the selectors hand out shape every downstream behaviour. If you select for compliant grade-grabbers, you cannot then complain that academia produces compliant grade-grabbers.

stories.summary: Amit recalls a story (referenced from a prior episode and the show notes) about how the great novelist Cormac McCarthy ended up copy-editing a research paper. The example demonstrates how dramatically a real writer can lift the prose of an academic paper.
stories.insight: Bad academic writing is a choice, not a fate. The same content, re-rendered in plain prose by someone who actually cares about clarity, becomes both better thinking and better communication. Every academic should study what good editing does to a paper.

stories.summary: Writing students often ask Amit why parts of Adam Smith's prose feel turgid. His answer: think about what Smith had available to read. He had a tiny pre-modern literature, no writing courses, no models for the prose values we take for granted. That he produced what he did from that thin training set makes the achievement greater, not lesser.
stories.insight: Modern creators stand on a vastly larger shoulder of giants. Anyone today, anywhere, can access the world's best writing and thinking. The privilege we now have is the historical anomaly, and complaining that 'masterpieces are rare' ignores how absurdly cheap the inputs have become.

stories.topic: From Times-Of-India Stringer To Self-Funded Podcaster
stories.summary: Amit walks through his own arc as a writer. In the 1990s, to publish a piece he had to send 800 words to the Times of India or Hindustan Times, accept a gatekeeper's biases, follow the news cycle, and watch the paper sell his eyeballs to advertisers for a tiny cut. As a blogger he could write any length on any topic with no gatekeeper. As a podcaster he could do eight-hour conversations with academics and be paid directly by listeners with no advertising middleman.
stories.insight: The means of production for ideas have collapsed in cost. A creator today can do what would have been laughed out of any 1990s pitch meeting (long-form audio, niche essay, audience-direct monetisation) and reach an audience across geography and across time. The gatekeepers' departure is the underrated story of the era.

stories.topic: Grigori Perelman Refuses The Million Dollars
stories.summary: Ajay tells the story of the great Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman, who lives in Moscow with his mother, walks in the forest and gathers mushrooms. After proving the Poincare conjecture, he posted the paper on arXiv and refused to publish in a journal: either the proof is right or it is wrong, no journal brand decides. When the Clay Mathematics Institute offered him their million-dollar award, he refused that too, on the grounds that prizes harm the collaboration DNA of the community by disproportionately rewarding one person who actually stood on many shoulders.
stories.insight: Perelman is not a hermit; he is making a structural argument. Authorship and credit, narrowly assigned, distort downstream incentives toward hoarding rather than sharing. The man who could not be bought turns out to be a teacher about the systems that buy us.

stories.summary: Amit gently pushes back on Ajay's blanket case against prizes. He won the Bastiat Prize in 2007 (second Indian ever) and again in 2015 (first person in the world to win it twice). It came at lonely moments: he was the only person in India writing about freedom in those terms; later he had quit writing for five years to play poker, returned to find he had been forgotten, and the second win and its $10,000 helped keep him going. The prize did not reward conformity; it rewarded exactly the opposite.
stories.insight: The case against prizes is real for monopolistic, elite-rewarding-elite prizes. But a free market in prizes is different. A thousand prizes for a thousand kinds of work, given by anyone who cares to put up money, can be a low-powered fertiliser for lonely strivers rather than a high-powered distortion.

recommendations.item: The Missionary Position: Mother Teresa in Theory and Practice
recommendations.creator: Christopher Hitchens
recommendations.context: Hitchens' polemical takedown of the Mother Teresa myth.
recommendations.reason: A masterclass in being suspicious of sanctimony. Amit misses Hitchens, who would have called out the bullshit on both left and right; reading him is training in how to challenge sacred cows with facts and logic rather than with deference.

recommendations.item: The Case Against Education
recommendations.creator: Bryan Caplan
recommendations.context: Caplan's data-driven argument that education is mostly signalling, not human-capital accumulation.
recommendations.reason: A book worth reading because the entire paradigm of school as a 19th-century factory for industrial workers is broken. We still rank fish by how well they climb trees. Caplan shows the magnitude of waste, even if the next paradigm is still up for grabs.

recommendations.item: Unelected Power
recommendations.creator: Paul Tucker
recommendations.context: Paul Tucker on the use of coercive power by unelected officials in advanced economies.
recommendations.reason: The first-world version of the administrative-state problem. Worth reading even from India because the same incentive failures, in milder form, illuminate our own administrative-state pathologies. A natural companion to Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic.

recommendations.item: Publish and Perish
recommendations.creator: Agnes Callard
recommendations.context: Callard's essay using economic-incentive thinking to explain why academic writing is so turgid.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Callard the best kind of public intellectual, always engaging on Twitter. The essay maps tenure-track economics onto why young academics are forced into deadening prose, and is the piece he gives his writing students stuck in academia.

recommendations.item: Politics and the English Language
recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Orwell's classic essay on plain English and the link between clear writing and clear thinking.
recommendations.reason: The two-way link is the lesson: clear thinking produces clear writing, but forcing yourself to write clearly forces you to think clearly. Whenever Amit meets unreadable academic prose, he assumes it is nonsense, and is normally right.

recommendations.item: Social Conformity Despite Individual Preferences for Distinctiveness
recommendations.creator: Paul Smaldino and Joshua Epstein
recommendations.context: A paper showing how conformity emerges even when individuals individually prefer to be distinctive.
recommendations.reason: The paper's title is the diagnosis. Young rebels enter university convinced they are independent thinkers, then conform to the toxic fashion of the day. Pair with Paul Graham's 'aggressively conventional-minded' to see why.

recommendations.item: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's framework dividing people on conventional-vs-independent and passive-vs-aggressive axes.
recommendations.reason: Provides Amit's working vocabulary for what is wrong with academia. The aggressively conventional-minded police the tribe and enforce fashions; you can spot them, name them, and route around them once you have the map.

recommendations.item: Marginal Revolution
recommendations.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: Cowen and Tabarrok's economics blog.
recommendations.reason: A live counter-example to the claim that academic writing must be turgid. Amit cites Cowen and Tabarrok as economists who write academic ideas in clear prose; if you are an academic looking for a model, this is one.

recommendations.item: Manifold Destiny
recommendations.creator: Sylvia Nasar and David Gruber
recommendations.context: A New Yorker piece on the proof of the Poincare conjecture and the fight over credit for it.
recommendations.reason: Background and depth on the Grigori Perelman story Ajay tells, and on why Perelman walked away from journals and the million-dollar Clay prize.

recommendations.item: Homeopathic Faith
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2010 essay on homeopathy.
recommendations.reason: A self-cited piece on why we should make fun of homeopathy. Used here as a model for being self-critical of one's own world; if you can mock pseudoscience outside, you should mock the hypocrisies of academia inside.

recommendations.item: If You Are a Creator, This Is Your Time
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's newsletter post on the creator economy.
recommendations.reason: Crystallises Amit's optimism: gatekeepers are dead, niches no one knew existed can find their audience, and a fifteen-year-old anywhere can build a body of work the world will discover. The case for the long game made directly.

recommendations.item: Do Prestigious Science Journals Attract Bad Science?
recommendations.creator: Julia Belluz
recommendations.context: Belluz in Vox surveying the evidence that high-prestige journals systematically attract worse science.
recommendations.reason: The empirical companion to Ajay's claim that the higher the journal, the lower the quality. People hack the journal-publication system harder where the rewards are highest, and the data backs up the gut intuition.

recommendations.item: DARPA
recommendations.creator: United States Department of Defense
recommendations.context: The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the US government's high-risk research funder.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's only example of a government funder that works fantastically well. Worth knowing about because most government research funding (especially in India) is captured by cronies; DARPA is what is possible when state capacity exists for meritocratic risk-taking.

recommendations.item: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books and One of the Most Influential Articles in Economics
recommendations.context: An account of how the novelist Cormac McCarthy ended up copy-editing a major economics paper.
recommendations.reason: A case study every academic should look at. It shows what real prose-editing does to a research paper and how much human-capital is left on the floor by the journal apparatus.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay and Kelkar's book on the art and science of economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommended as the deeper Indian-context companion to Paul Tucker's Unelected Power. Where Tucker writes about administrative-state pathologies in advanced economies, this book treats the harder Indian version of the same problem.

recommendations.item: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Episode 22, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A previous EIE episode on firms and how they move forward.
recommendations.reason: Backlinked because the episode treats firms as the central productive units of modern society and the consumers who can fund meritocratic research, the one piece of the funding stack Ajay says works.

recommendations.item: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on finance.
recommendations.reason: Backlinked because finance is Ajay's example of the rare part of economics where for-profit firms fund and use academic work, producing a healthy meritocratic feedback loop between research and practice.

recommendations.item: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Episode 3, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode whose Chapter 4 covered hydroponics.
recommendations.reason: Linked because that earlier hydroponics riff is what makes the in-show joke about being self-critical land. If you can mock hydroponics, you can mock your own institutions.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek (Episode 6, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on Frederic Bastiat and Friedrich Hayek.
recommendations.reason: Linked because the Bastiat Prize is named after one of Amit's heroes and motivates his defence of prizes, and because Bastiat is one of the seen-and-unseen ancestors of the show's framing.

recommendations.item: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Episode 19, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on cricket and decision-making.
recommendations.reason: Linked because Ajay reuses its core insight here: marginal contribution to win-probability matters only when it bubbles up to the selectors. Selectors are the root cause in cricket teams and in academic departments alike.

recommendations.item: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (Episode 321, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Josh Felman
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen-and-the-Unseen conversation with the economist Josh Felman.
recommendations.reason: Linked because Felman is the friend who supplied the BMW-off-a-cliff metaphor for American college costs.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen-and-the-Unseen episode with Ajay on Ukraine and Russia.
recommendations.reason: Linked because the discussion of strategy, operations, and tactics on this episode draws on the military-affairs grounding worked out at length there.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (Episode 349, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Timur Kuran
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen-and-the-Unseen episode with Timur Kuran.
recommendations.reason: Linked because Kuran's work on waqfs as institutions whose original purposes have decayed is the analogy for old universities sitting on capital that is no longer doing the job it was meant to do.

recommendations.item: Sturgeon's Law
recommendations.context: The aphorism, attributed to the science-fiction writer Theodore Sturgeon, that ninety percent of everything is crap.
recommendations.reason: Cited as the standard reply to the complaint that creator-economy content is mostly bad. Of course it is; ninety percent of everything always was. The point is that today anyone can be in the ten percent without asking permission.

recommendations.item: The Bastiat Prize
recommendations.context: An annual prize for journalism in defence of free societies.
recommendations.reason: Self-referenced because Amit won it twice. He uses it as the live counter-example to Ajay's case against prizes: a non-elite, ideologically-specific prize that meaningfully helped a lonely writer continue his work.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's writing course.
recommendations.reason: Mentioned as the context where he teaches students to write clearly even when their academic environments demand turgid prose. The course is the practical companion to the Orwell-Callard line of argument in the episode.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Pillars Of A Knowledge Society
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's organising frame for the entire episode. Every knowledge-producing institution has three distinct missions: making new knowledge (research), diffusing knowledge (teaching, public discourse, journalism, podcasts), and applying knowledge to make the world better (firms, policy, governance). A board member of any university should ask of all three: are we doing this well? The current diagnosis is that none of the three works as it should.
core_ideas.quote: We are here to make knowledge, to diffuse knowledge, and to link up knowledge to action.

core_ideas.concept: The Journal Process Is Capture, Not Quality
core_ideas.explanation: Researchers no longer ask 'what is an important problem?' but 'how do I hack into the editor and the referee?' A germ of an idea that takes a week mutates into a five-to-eight-year publication ordeal of dressing-up and revising-to-taste with no creative value added. The fashions of editors and referees exert disproportionate influence; other researchers behave as lemmings. Ironically, the higher the journal, the lower the quality of the underlying paper, because the people willing to game hardest get in. Most published papers are never cited and 362 of 365 days a year are spent on schmoozing and revising rather than thinking.
core_ideas.quote: It is ironic that the higher the journal, the lower the quality.

core_ideas.concept: Three Funders, Only One Of Which Works
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's taxonomy: corporate, government, and philanthropic funding. Corporations work because they are meritocratic and want shit done at well-defined problems. Government funding mostly fails because it is a state-capacity problem (DARPA being the rare exception). Philanthropy fails for two reasons: it is captured by feel-good humanitarian goals (cyclones photograph better than abstract science) and it is run by risk-averse bureaucrats protecting their job security rather than venture-capital-style risk-takers. James Watt did more for India's poor than Mother Teresa, but no philanthropist sees the link.
core_ideas.quote: James Watt arguably did more for poor people in India than Mother Teresa, but most philanthropists are not sufficiently intellectual to see these links.

core_ideas.concept: Credentialism Is The Disease Of Diffusion
core_ideas.explanation: Universities have collapsed pillar two of the knowledge society into the production of brand-name diplomas. Students do not want the knowledge; they want the chhaap that gets them a job at Google. Universities have responded by raising fees and competing on five-star resort facilities. The kindling-of-imagination function has been pushed aside because no party in the transaction is paying for it. In economics terms, the value of an IIT graduate's life is mostly intrinsic capability; the brand name's incremental value is small but employer information failures keep it bid up.
core_ideas.quote: You get a Louis Vuitton bag, it is some IIT degree, and then you're supposed to be done.

core_ideas.concept: Education Is Kindling A Fire, Not Filling A Pail
core_ideas.explanation: The model where you finish learning at twenty-two and then live off the diploma was an industrial-era construct from a world where people retired at fifty-five. With longevity now reaching one hundred and twenty, the only sane construct is lifelong learning. Knowledge is slow; the universe reveals itself bit by bit; you can pass any exam without truly understanding. Add the fact that the world itself changes faster than any career, and rigid four-year compression looks doubly absurd. Build the institutions, the cultures and the personal habits for lifelong learning instead.
core_ideas.quote: The process of education is not filling a pail, the process of education is kindling a fire.

core_ideas.concept: The Selectors Are The Root Cause
core_ideas.explanation: A through-line Ajay borrows from his own work on cricket: the marginal-contribution-to-win-probability of a player only matters when it shapes selection. Apply the same lens to the knowledge society and the deepest dysfunctions are at the level of the selectors: who picks PhD students, who hires faculty, who promotes them, who funds research, who runs admissions. Whatever incentives the selectors hand out shape every downstream behaviour. The way to fix things is to fix the management decisions at the selection layer, not to scold individual researchers for responding to the incentives they were given.
core_ideas.quote: Some of the most broken things in the intellectual world are the selection process.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's frame for pillar three. Connecting knowledge to the world requires every firm and government to put a microscope on itself, not just incrementally turn screws like a process engineer. It needs a continuous self-argument about who we are, what we are doing wrong, where we will be in five or ten years. The execution-only orientation is the slide to mediocrity. All too often firms and governments instead reduce to a contest for power, then the winner shuts down internal discourse to protect themselves: 'I'm in charge, you can't criticise anything we are doing.'

Borrowed from Orwell. The link is two-way: clear thinkers write more clearly, but forcing yourself to write clearly also forces you to think clearly, because abstract jargon is where vagueness hides. Amit's working heuristic: when academic prose is hard to read, assume it is nonsense (it normally is). The duty falls on every academic who has real ideas to also be a public intellectual, communicating in clear and explicable prose, because the bar to do so is now zero.
core_ideas.quote: Whenever I come across a piece of academia that is difficult to read, I assume it is nonsense and it is normally nonsense.

core_ideas.explanation: The means of production for ideas have collapsed in price. Where once a writer needed a newspaper, an audio creator needed a radio company, and a researcher needed a journal, now anyone can publish, podcast, livestream, or post a paper to arXiv. Niches no one knew existed find their audiences directly. Eight-hour conversations with academics, monetised by listener subscriptions rather than advertising, would have been laughed out of any 1990s pitch meeting. The mainstream is crumbling, and that is good news.
core_ideas.quote: Anyone who has the hunger and the spark can go out there and gain knowledge.

core_ideas.concept: Communities Of Choice Replace Communities Of Circumstance
core_ideas.explanation: Across most of human history your ideas were shaped by whoever lived in physical proximity to you. The internet, despite its toxicity, lets you wake up every morning and have a look at what the best minds in the world are thinking about, all of them thinking aloud for your benefit. That is fucking magic compared to even twenty years ago. Most of Amit's friends are people he met because of the internet; the same will be true for any creative person willing to curate.
core_ideas.quote: Twenty years ago this would have been magic.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's argument, taken from Grigori Perelman: prizes give excessively disproportionate rewards to the one runner who took the baton across the finish line, and so re-shape the incentives of everyone else. If you and I are racing for a Nobel, you hoard your ideas and I hoard mine; we cooperate less; the whole community produces less. The cure is low-powered incentives rather than high-powered ones, broader notions of authorship that include the bicycle-repair-shop conversation, and a willingness to play down the cult of the lone author.
core_ideas.quote: If you and I are in a race for a Nobel Prize, then I'll be hoarding my ideas and you'll be hoarding your ideas.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's friendly amendment. The case against prizes is right when prizes are monopolistic and elite-rewarding-elite (he refuses on principle to take any government award). But a free market in prizes, where anyone can put up money for any kind of work, is different. Lonely strivers in unfashionable directions can be quietly fertilised by people who care about that direction. The Bastiat Prize meant a great deal to him in two career moments precisely because it rewarded going against the Indian intellectual fashion, not with it. Let a thousand prizes bloom rather than abolish prizes.

core_ideas.concept: We Are Playing The Long Game
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's framing for what creators are actually doing. Building a repository, building communities of thinkers, reaching out across geography (which a professor in a college cannot) and across time (which yesterday's media could not). When he started The Seen and the Unseen he wanted someone thirty years later to listen and get an insight into this world and these people. The fifteen-year-old in some remote town in India who will be prime minister in thirty years is now getting her knowledge from YouTube, podcasts, and books a previous era could not have delivered. That is the real audience.

Amit borrows Timur Kuran's analysis of waqfs in the Middle East and applies it to old universities. A waqf set up to build water fountains becomes purposeless once piped water arrives, but its capital is locked up. Modern universities sit on enormous endowments and on a wider unseen credit that they are still 'where the best and the brightest' work. Both are, increasingly, dead capital. Lots of resources, real and reputational, are tied up there doing a job they no longer do.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay teases Amit at the open: 'I'm a card-carrying economist, I've done a PhD and all of that. You studied nothing, you're a fool' before conceding the whole episode that degrees mean nothing.
Amit, deadpan, on Ajay's rant about Indian heat in the patent office: 'Edison didn't have air conditioning in his office.' Ajay: 'Yeah, and his cameras did not overheat in the Indian heat. Carry on.'
Josh Felman's image for the cost of US college, retold by Ajay: 'putting one child through college in America involves buying one brand-new BMW car every year and rolling it off the edge of a cliff.'
Ajay, on the credential as luxury good: 'You get a Louis Vuitton bag, it is some IIT degree, and then you're supposed to be done.'

Amit on the absurd Indian PhD-application logic: a paper on 'wheat production in Arizona between the years eighteen sixty-three to eighteen sixty-five' as an example of the silos academics dig themselves into.
Amit on schools designed for the industrial revolution: 'monkeys can climb trees, but you're also putting fish through an exam of how to climb trees.'
Amit on government prizes: 'oh, you government bureaucrat, you wanna give me a Padma Shri? Fuck off. The Khan Market Liberal Award will never be accepted by me.'
Amit, defending his Bastiat winnings against Ajay's prize-abolitionism: 'do not take my two candlesticks away from me.'
Amit's verdict on academia: 'It's pompous old farts talking to other pompous old farts.'

Ajay, mid-flow, putting himself in Amit's role: 'Captain Varma, where are you giving us your great books? When are you going to produce a movie for us? I will say, you know, shut up and get me the movie.'
'Publication orientation' - the dreaded phrase older academics use to beat the idealism out of new researchers: shut up, sit down and write the paper, get me the pub.
'Circle of Niceness' - Agnes Callard's term for the mutually-flattering citation economy among academics, invoked by Amit as the engine of turgid prose.
Sturgeon's Law - the science-fiction-writer's aphorism that ninety percent of everything is crap, used to deflate the standard complaint about the creator economy.

Edison: 'genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration', invoked by Ajay to acknowledge the legitimate hard work that goes into research, before arguing the balance has tipped from creation to administration.
'The process of education is not filling a pail, the process of education is kindling a fire' - the Yeats-attributed line used by Ajay as the slogan for lifelong learning over credentialism.
'And if you listen very hard, the tune will come to you at last' - Led Zeppelin's 'Stairway to Heaven', used by Ajay to make the point that real knowledge takes a lifetime of attention to surface.
Picasso did not invent cubism out of thin air - Ajay's reminder that authorship is dispersed and that the lone-genius story flatters the namesake at the expense of the surrounding scene.

Grigori Perelman - the mushroom-gathering Moscow mathematician who refused to publish in journals and refused the Clay Institute's million-dollar prize, used here as the moral exemplar of distrust of the credit-and-prize machinery.
Frederic Bastiat - the seen-and-the-unseen economist whose name lives on in the Bastiat Prize and is invoked by Amit as one of his heroes.

Timur Kuran on waqfs - mid-east religious endowments tied to obsolete missions, repurposed by Amit as the analogy for elite universities sitting on endowments while no longer doing the job they were built to do.

Vajpayee circa 2002-2003 on the knowledge economy - Ajay's recalled speech in which the then-Prime-Minister argued that knowledge should fill every pore of our bodies, cast aside individual superstition, and feed firms and the state alike.

'I won, and I won big ones, and I paid the cost. Inside, I felt like I was carrying the broken spirits of all the other ones who lost' - the songwriter line Ajay quotes to anchor his case against high-powered prize incentives.
